questions.question: How does @InjectMocks injection work under the hood?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Injection Strategy | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **@InjectMocks tries three injection strategies in order:** constructor injection (match by type), setter injection, then field injection. If none succeed, it creates the object with no injection — no error is thrown, leading to null fields that cause NPE at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of @InjectMocks understanding and its failure modes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not understanding why @InjectMocks silently fails to inject when there's no matching constructor
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the silent failure mode and why explicit constructor construction is sometimes safer

sections.title: Three-Strategy Injection with Silent Failure
sections.content: Mockito tries in order: (1) **Constructor injection**: finds a constructor whose parameter types match @Mock fields. Creates instance via that constructor. (2) **Setter injection**: finds setters for @Mock types. (3) **Field injection**: injects directly into private fields via reflection. **Silent failure**: if none succeed, Mockito creates the object (via no-arg constructor) without injecting — no error. The @InjectMocks field has an instance but its dependencies are null.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Constructor injection: preferred — explicit dependency contract
- Setter injection: secondary — requires setters
- Field injection: last resort — relies on reflection, bypasses Java visibility
- Silent failure: no exception if injection fails — NPE at runtime
- Spring-style constructor injection works best with @InjectMocks
- @InjectMocks can't handle final fields or primitive constructor args
- Consider: explicit new ClassUnderTest(mockDep1, mockDep2) — more debuggable
- @InjectMocks doesn't work if class has multiple constructors with ambiguity

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @InjectMocks tries constructor injection first — it looks for a constructor whose parameter types match the @Mock fields in the test class. If that works, great. If not, it tries setter injection, then field injection via reflection. The critical danger is silent failure: if no strategy succeeds, Mockito creates the object with its no-arg constructor and doesn't inject anything, without throwing an error. You only discover this when the test throws a NullPointerException at the point where the dependency is used. This is why I sometimes prefer explicitly writing new OrderService(mockRepository, mockEmailService) — it fails loudly if parameters don't match.

questions.question: Should you use field injection or constructor injection in production Spring services?
questions.title: Field vs Constructor Injection Spring | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Prefer constructor injection over @Autowired field injection.** Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, enables immutable final fields, works with @InjectMocks in tests without extra tools, and fails fast if a dependency is missing — at startup rather than at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Spring best practices and testability — an opinion question where the right answer is well-established
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defending field injection because it requires less code — missing the testability and immutability benefits of constructor injection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect testability: constructor injection enables @InjectMocks to work cleanly without Mockito reflection tricks

sections.title: Constructor Injection is the Best Practice
sections.content: **Field injection** (`@Autowired private OrderRepository repo`): short but relies on Spring reflection. Can't use outside Spring context. Dependencies not visible in constructor. @InjectMocks might use field injection as last resort. **Constructor injection**: `@Service public class OrderService { private final OrderRepository repo; @Autowired OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } }`. With Lombok: `@RequiredArgsConstructor` generates the constructor. Immutable final fields, testable without Mockito hacks.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Constructor injection: explicit, final, testable, fails at startup
- Field injection: concise, but hidden dependencies, mutable, harder to test
- Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor: generates constructor automatically
- Spring 4.3+: single constructor auto-wired without @Autowired annotation
- @InjectMocks: works best with constructor injection
- Spring team recommends constructor injection
- Circular dependency: constructor injection fails at startup (good!)
- Setter injection: for optional dependencies

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I prefer constructor injection. It makes all dependencies explicit — anyone reading the class knows exactly what it needs. Fields can be final and immutable. If a required dependency is missing, the application fails at startup with a clear error rather than at runtime. For testing, constructor injection works cleanly with @InjectMocks and also makes it trivial to create the class manually in tests. The downside is more boilerplate, which I eliminate with Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor. Spring's own documentation recommends constructor injection, and it's the approach I use for all mandatory dependencies.

questions.title: Manual Mock Injection Without @InjectMocks | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: **Create the class under test manually in @BeforeEach, passing mocks as constructor arguments.** This is explicit, debuggable, and fails loudly if arguments don't match. Preferred for complex setups where @InjectMocks silent failure would be hard to debug.

sections.title: Explicit Construction in @BeforeEach
Key Points
sections.content:
- @BeforeEach: create new instance with mocks as constructor args
- No @InjectMocks annotation needed
- Fails at compile time if constructor changes — safer
- More verbose but explicit and debuggable
- @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) still needed for @Mock

- When to prefer @InjectMocks: standard Spring service with single constructor

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Instead of @InjectMocks, I can create the class under test explicitly in @BeforeEach by passing the mock fields as constructor arguments. This is completely transparent — anyone reading the test immediately sees what dependencies are being injected. If the constructor signature changes, the test fails at compile time with a clear error rather than at runtime with a NullPointerException. I tend to use this approach when debugging @InjectMocks issues or when the class has complex construction logic. @InjectMocks is convenient for the common case of a Spring service with a single obvious constructor.

questions.question: What is @MockBean in Spring Boot testing and how does it differ from @Mock?
questions.title: @MockBean vs @Mock Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **@MockBean** replaces a bean in the Spring application context with a Mockito mock. **@Mock** creates a standalone Mockito mock without loading Spring. Use @Mock for unit tests (fast), @MockBean for integration tests where the Spring context must be loaded.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring Boot testing knowledge — understanding context boundaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean in unit tests — unnecessarily loads the Spring context, making tests slow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @MockBean invalidates the Spring context cache, causing re-load — a performance concern in large test suites

sections.title: Context-Level vs Standalone Mocking
sections.content: **@Mock** (Mockito): standalone fake, no Spring context. Fast — milliseconds. Used with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class). **@MockBean** (Spring Boot Test): injects a Mockito mock into the Spring ApplicationContext, replacing the real bean. Requires @SpringBootTest or a slice test (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest). Slow — seconds — because it loads/re-loads the context. Use @MockBean only when you need the context; use @Mock for unit tests.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @Mock: no Spring, fast, for unit tests
- @MockBean: replaces Spring bean, for integration tests
- @MockBean used with: @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest
- @MockBean invalidates Spring context cache — causes re-load
- Never use @MockBean for unit tests — unnecessary context loading
- @SpyBean: Spring equivalent of @Spy
- @MockBean auto-reset after each test
- Performance: minimize @MockBean usage to preserve context cache

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @Mock creates a standalone Mockito mock with no Spring involved — fast, for unit tests. @MockBean is a Spring Boot extension that replaces a real bean in the Spring application context with a Mockito mock. I use @MockBean in integration tests with @SpringBootTest or slice tests like @WebMvcTest when I need the full context but want to replace specific beans. The key performance concern is that each unique combination of @MockBean beans can invalidate Spring's context cache, causing it to re-load — which is slow. So I use @Mock wherever possible and only reach for @MockBean when I genuinely need the context.

questions.question: What happens when @InjectMocks cannot inject a mock?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Silent Injection Failure
questions.direct_answer: Mockito silently skips the injection and leaves the field null, causing NullPointerException in tests; using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with strict stubs helps surface these issues earlier.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you are aware of this silent failure mode that causes confusing NullPointerExceptions in tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming @InjectMocks will throw a clear error if injection fails — it does not, it silently continues
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that strict stubbing mode helps indirectly by failing on unused stubs, and that constructor injection in production code avoids this entirely

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
This is one of the most frustrating gotchas with @InjectMocks. When Mockito cannot find a suitable mock to inject into a field of the class under test, it does not throw an exception — it silently leaves the field as null. Your test class will be created successfully, and only when a test method actually tries to use that null dependency will you get a NullPointerException, which can be very confusing to debug.

This typically happens when field names or types do not match what Mockito expects, when you forget to declare the @Mock for a required dependency, or when the class under test was refactored and a new dependency was added but no corresponding @Mock was created in the test.

The best defense is to use constructor injection in your production code. When your class takes its dependencies through a constructor, Mockito must use constructor injection, and if the constructor parameters cannot be matched to available mocks, the error is much more obvious.

Additionally, using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with strict stubbing helps catch related issues — it will report unused stubs, which can indicate that the mock you created was never used because injection failed. But there is no complete automatic detection of silent null injection outside of writing your tests carefully and keeping production code constructor-injected.

The symptom is NullPointerException in the test at the point where the uninjected dependency is used
Prefer constructor injection in production code to make injection failures obvious
Strict stubbing mode catches unused stubs which can indicate failed injection

questions.question: How does Mockito decide between constructor injection and field injection for @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Constructor vs Field Injection in @InjectMocks
questions.direct_answer: Mockito tries constructor injection first (using the largest constructor that matches available mocks), then setter injection, then field injection as a fallback.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Mockito's injection resolution order and why constructor injection is the safest option
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Mockito always uses field injection; not knowing that constructor injection is attempted first and is safer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect this to Spring's own injection preference: constructor injection is favored in both production Spring code and Mockito tests for the same reason — it makes dependencies explicit

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Mockito's @InjectMocks follows a specific three-step resolution process. First it attempts constructor injection: it looks for the largest constructor and tries to match available @Mock fields to the constructor parameters by type and name. If it finds a match it uses that constructor. Second, if no suitable constructor is found, it tries setter injection: it looks for setter methods that match available mocks. Third, as a last resort it falls back to field injection using reflection, directly setting private fields.

Constructor injection is the safest option for several reasons. When your class has a constructor that explicitly declares its dependencies, any missing mock will cause a clear failure rather than a silent null. It also aligns perfectly with how Spring itself recommends writing production code — use constructor injection in your @Service and @Component classes, and both Spring and Mockito will work predictably.

Field injection, while convenient, hides the dependencies of a class. A class with ten @Autowired fields does not advertise its coupling at all, and in tests this means Mockito silently injects what it can and leaves the rest null.

As a best practice: write your production services with constructor injection, which makes your @InjectMocks tests more reliable, your classes more testable, and your dependencies more visible in code review.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Mockito injection order: constructor injection → setter injection → field injection
Constructor injection is preferred — failures are explicit, not silent
Field injection uses reflection to set private fields; silent failures are common
Aligns with Spring's recommendation: use constructor injection in @Service classes

questions.question: How do you test a class that uses constructor injection without @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Manual Constructor Injection in Tests
questions.direct_answer: Create the mocks with @Mock or Mockito.mock(), then pass them directly to the class constructor in @BeforeEach — no @InjectMocks needed, and the wiring is explicit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that @InjectMocks is a convenience, not a requirement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying on @InjectMocks silently failing when a dependency is missing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Advocate for explicit constructor injection in tests as the most transparent and debuggable approach

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
@InjectMocks is a convenience annotation, but it has a well-known problem: if Mockito cannot inject a dependency, it silently skips it and leaves the field as null, causing NullPointerExceptions in the test rather than a clear setup failure.

The explicit alternative is to create mocks and pass them to the constructor yourself in @BeforeEach. Suppose you have an OrderService(OrderRepository repository, EmailSender emailSender). In your test class you write @Mock OrderRepository mockRepository; @Mock EmailSender mockEmailSender; private OrderService orderService; and then in @BeforeEach you write orderService = new OrderService(mockRepository, mockEmailSender). This is completely explicit — the compiler tells you if you add a new dependency and forget to update the test, unlike @InjectMocks which would silently leave it null.

This approach also makes the test more readable. When a colleague sees new OrderService(mockRepository, mockEmailSender) in the setup method, the dependencies are immediately obvious without needing to understand Mockito's injection rules.

Most experienced developers prefer explicit constructor injection in unit tests. @InjectMocks is acceptable for small, stable classes but becomes a maintenance risk as classes evolve. If you are on a team that uses Checkstyle or SpotBugs, some configurations warn against @InjectMocks for exactly this reason.

content: Create mocks with @Mock, then call new MyService(mock1, mock2) in @BeforeEach.
Explicit constructor injection catches missing dependencies at compile time.
@InjectMocks silently skips unresolved dependencies, leading to confusing NPEs.
Prefer explicit wiring for clarity and maintainability.
